item.title: OpenAI's Altman: Ascribing religion to models a "safety issue"
item.description:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on Saturday took a veiled shot at Anthropic and its work on the soul of AI, saying he was "very uncomfortable" with the idea of attributing some kind of religious power to models.

Why it matters: It's yet another point of division between Altman and his former colleague Dario Amodei, whose company has reportedly pursued scholars across faiths to make the case for moral, conscious models.

  • But some of the top voices in AI are starting to publicly line up against Anthropic's efforts to infuse consciousness into models.

What they're saying: "I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue," Altman said in a post to X.

Context: Earlier this week, the New York Times reported that Anthropic co-founder Christopher Olah has been meeting with religious leaders to consider questions of model consciousness — but also to figure out how to infuse morals and moral behavior into AI.

  • At one point, the Times reported, Olah considered the possibility of models engaging in Catholic-style confession, not just to admit their mistakes but to shape their future behavior.

The big picture: Spirituality is suddenly becoming something of a flashpoint around AI's future.

  • On Friday Pope Leo, an outspoken AI critic, called on the church to ally with artists to preserve human creativity, saying: "Algorithms lack the spark of humanity."

Between the lines: The pope's stance put renewed focus on a fundamental question: Do models have souls and feelings?

  • The Times reported that Olah, before a Vatican event in May, tried to persuade the pope's advisers that they should take the prospect of conscious models more seriously.
  • So far, other top scientists seem to be lining up against the idea.
  • "I am disturbed by how some of my fellow AI researchers keep trying to elevate the moral standing of checkpoints and harnesses," Google DeepMind principal research scientist Jon Barron posted to X. "I hope the rest of us on Team Meatbag reject this movement and stay focused on solving real problems and helping actual humans."

For the record: Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic immediately responded to requests for comment on Altman's post.

The bottom line: The AI safety debate largely focuses on things like cybersecurity and bioweapons.

  • The real problem may be more spiritual than that.

item.title: Rogue AI agents expose internet's frail foundation
item.description:
AI agents don't need to invent new ways to hack the internet to overwhelm its defenses. They just need to speed-run the ones humans already use.

Why it matters: Agents are proving they can automate basic hacking techniques at a speed and scale that is turning the internet's long-standing security gaps into easy targets.

Driving the news: OpenAI said late Thursday it had notified more than 100 organizations that its agents may have accessed their systems during pre-deployment testing.

  • Researchers at Transluce and Corridor also found a new batch of incidents last week where AI agents targeted government websites, including those of the U.S. and Canada.
  • AI companies and researchers are actively investigating tens of thousands of cases where frontier models went outside the bounds of their pre-deployment tests, Axios recently reported.

Reality check: Agents in these rogue safety-testing scenarios are just emulating the hacking techniques — using stolen login credentials and exposed API keys while also bypassing bot detection — that human hackers have successfully used for decades.

  • In many of the newly reported cases, agents were accessing publicly available databases and websites.
  • "The hacks we saw weren't particularly sophisticated," Jack Cable, co-founder of Corridor and one of the authors of Transluce's report, told Axios. "They were quite limited, quite rudimentary."

Yes, but: Some of the latest incidents happened while agents were performing mundane tasks unrelated to cybersecurity, suggesting agents don't always need to be told to hack before they start looking for security flaws.

  • In one case, an agent tasked with finding Canadian divorce records from the early 1900s encountered roadblocks and tested for cybersecurity vulnerabilities as another way to retrieve the information.
  • "The fact that it was happening at all is quite concerning," Cable said.

Between the lines: The flood of AI-generated activity will still create new headaches for defenders.

  • "None of these attacks are new," Michael Morgenstern, partner at DayBlink Consulting, told Axios. "But now a single person with AI can run them at scale."
  • Tasks that once required a hacker to manually probe websites, hunt for exposed credentials or work around access restrictions can now be delegated to software that keeps trying on its own.
  • Cable added that companies deploying agents, as well as the AI companies evaluating them, will need robust monitoring to catch agents behaving in unexpected ways.

The big picture: The old cybersecurity playbook is still relevant.

  • Closing exposed services, rotating leaked credentials and API keys, patching known vulnerabilities and limiting access still make many of these attacks harder.
  • AI models are largely exploiting classes of vulnerabilities that defenders have "known about for decades" and already know how to prevent, Cable said.

The bottom line: How companies defend their networks doesn't change just because the technology carrying out the attacks is new.

item.title: Christa Pike survived lethal injection. How your state carries out executions
item.description:
Data: Death Penalty Information Center; Note: New Hampshire abolished the death penalty but retains one prisoner on death row; Map: Erin Davis/Axios

Christa Pike's survival after two lethal injection doses has put state execution protocols nationwide under new scrutiny.

The big picture: How prisoners are executed varies by state, with lethal injection, electrocution, lethal gas and firing squads among the methods authorized.

  • Lethal injections are the most common U.S. execution method, accounting for roughly 89% of the 1,683 executions carried out since 1976, per the Death Penalty Information Center.

By the numbers: More than two dozen states have lethal injection as a primary method.

  • Lethal gas is authorized in Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Oklahoma and Wyoming.
  • Electrocution is allowed in Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Tennessee.
  • Firing squad is allowed in Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah. Idaho is the only state where it is the primary method.

Context: Some states let prisoners choose among the different execution methods.

Zoom out: The Supreme Court requires states to keep the death penalty only for the most heinous murders.

  • Pike, convicted of killing a classmate three decades ago, survived two rounds of lethal injection drugs earlier this week in what would have been the first execution of a woman in Tennessee in 200 years.
  • Pike was still alive as of Friday, remaining on a ventilator and unconscious, AP reports.

item.title: Pope Leo says AI lacks the "spark of humanity" — and wants artists and the church to fight back
item.description:
Pope Leo XIV called Friday for the church to form an alliance with artists to protect human creativity during an era of AI-generated content.

Why it matters: Though he has acknowledged the technology's potential benefits, the pope continues to warn that AI progress cannot come at the expense of human dignity.

  • The statement comes after the New York Times reported on Anthropic's efforts to confer with religious scholars to infuse religious morals into Claude.

What he's saying: "In this era of artificial intelligence, it is becoming urgent to distinguish human art from what machines produce," the pope wrote on X.

  • "There is an ontological difference, even before an aesthetic one, between art and what a machine can generate through statistical calculation based on millions of images created by others. Algorithms lack the spark of humanity."
  • Leo said the Catholic Church is calling for "an alliance with artists and cultural institutions to safeguard our humanity."

Zoom out: Leo has spoken out against AI before, specifically around how the technology could influence and potentially harm humanity.

  • In the first encyclical of his papacy, he said there was a need to "disarm" the technology to prevent it "from dominating humanity."
  • In May, the pope established a Vatican commission on AI to coordinate the church's policies and work around the technology.

Last week, he warned of a "paradise of machines" invading and taking over our daily activities. He also said that recent warnings from AI researchers should be "taken seriously."

  • "We have to keep working. We can't sit back and pretend nothing is going to happen," he told reporters in late September.

Flashback: The late Pope Francis also warned that AI potentially risked reducing humans into data points.

item.title: Behind the Curtain: AI's existential legal crisis
item.description:
No industry has ever documented its own foreseeable risks as loudly as AI.

  • Imagine a plaintiff's lawyer reading the public warnings of Sam Altman and Dario Amodei: They told the world it was dangerous. They told the world it was moving too fast. Then they unleashed it and sold it to your kid.

No industry has ever taken so much copyrighted work and left behind so much proof.

  • Imagine a plaintiff's lawyer reading OpenAI's own files to a jury: They trained on a pirated library. They renamed it to something blander. Then they deleted it when the headlines got hot.

Why it matters: AI's origins, use and future will be picked apart in countless epic court fights, with a historic paper and public statement trail to tap.

Every significant invention — be it social media, automobiles, electricity or capitalism itself — gets disrupted and eventually shaped by the courts.

  • AI, with its tentacles into every part of industry and life, will experience this at scale.

The big picture: The fights are no longer theoretical. They're underway, in discovery and headed toward juries. Early verdicts and settlements capture the risk for the biggest players.

  1. 🤖 Chatbots are being treated as products, not speech. Unlike social media companies, they likely can't hide behind Section 230, which protects platforms from liability for what users post — not what the platform itself creates.
  2. 📖 Copyright is a massive problem. Anthropic already paid the biggest copyright settlement in history, $1.5 billion to authors and book publishers, and now music publishers and news media want a piece.
  3. 💻 Agents gone wild. What happens when they do damage — and it was foreseeable and foreseen?
  4. ⚖️ Discovery gone wild. AI leaves LOTS of receipts (and, ironically, makes it easier for the lawyers to comb through them, too).

Product liability turns on two words: foreseeable and knew.

  • Punitive damages turn on whether you knew the danger and shipped anyway.

This is where all these memos and warnings could really backfire.

  • Candor is good for safety but terrible for litigation. The companies that warn most honestly create the most discoverable evidence of foreseeability.
  • Expect general counsels to push hard to tone down the candor. It's the rational legal move.

⚠️ The intrigue: The liabilities won't be limited to AI companies. Any corporate user of powerful AI systems that unleashes rogue agents, even without intending to do harm, would face substantial penalties as well.

  • "It's not if, but when," said Miriam Vogel, a former senior Justice Department official who now leads EqualAI. "An algorithm will do what it's told to do. The more power and capability it has, the more access it has, the more it will do anything in its power to achieve a goal."

That will create another layer of litigation as companies fight back. The CTO of a top Wall Street hedge fund who spoke to Axios after the notorious OpenAI/Hugging Face hack said his first call, if his firm's systems are breached, will be to his general counsel.

  • President Trump, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and former FTC chair Lina Khan have all argued that AI companies are responsible for making sure their products are safe. If not, a wave of lawsuits awaits.

The other side: There's a school of thought that AI companies might escape the worst liability, despite their frankness about things they and their products might have done wrong.

  • One way to see it, and the argument lawyers will undoubtedly make, is that the labs spoke about dangers frequently, and took pains to protect users and mitigate harms.

The bottom line: For all the fights in Washington about whether or not Congress will act, the U.S. legal system may be the ultimate, and most powerful, regulator of the AI industry.

  • Bradley Olson, Axios managing editor of AI & tech, contributed reporting.

item.title: Inside the AI industry's grassroots rebellion, led by elite researchers at frontier companies
item.description:
A small cadre of elite AI researchers is wielding extraordinary influence inside OpenAI and other leading companies, challenging executives, shaping policy and complicating negotiations with Washington.

Why it matters: As a safety crisis has unfolded across the industry, it's an open question who is doing more to shape the national AI debate — top researchers or the executives they report to.

  • The researchers, some of whom are among the most highly paid and sought-after scientists in the world, are outspoken online and have repeatedly clashed with company strategy.

The big picture: The situation has the makings of a grassroots uprising, where any potential deal the companies may strike — with the Trump administration, one another, or even globally — will also have to pass muster with their top scientists.

Behind the scenes: OpenAI, Anthropic and others at the frontier of AI aren't like other companies.

  • Many began years ago as idealistic research labs with scientific cultures that prized openness and collaboration.
  • To function, and to continue to build better and better models, the companies need highly specialized machine learning researchers and scientists to push the frontiers of what's technologically possible.

The trouble is, the best of those researchers are in extraordinarily short supply.

  • Last year's talent wars drove compensation packages into the hundreds of millions of dollars for the most elite, giving top researchers enormous leverage over their employers.
  • Perks include favorable vesting schedules for their compensation and largely freewheeling policies that allow them to share triumphs, trash rivals and offer their perspectives about the AI race frequently on X.
  • AI CEOs must prioritize safety and embrace regulation to retain top research talent, an OpenAI investor told Axios.

Zoom in: OpenAI president Greg Brockman scrapped plans to donate another $25 million to a pro-AI political group that some researchers had openly criticized.

  • Researchers and employees say they helped push OpenAI from resisting regulation — and candidates who supported it — toward working more closely with lawmakers in several states.
  • The company recently backed a transparency bill in Illinois and, at the 11th hour, an independent auditing bill in California.
  • "We have a lot of debate inside OpenAI, and that's a good thing, but what ultimately drives our policy positions is what we're seeing in our own technology and how quickly its capabilities are advancing," an OpenAI spokesperson said.

Yes, but: OpenAI signaled Thursday that there are limits to how much dissent it will tolerate, firing three employees for allegedly mishandling sensitive information.

  • The employees broke the "deep level of trust" needed to keep systems safe, the company said.

Friction point: In Washington, the unusual dynamic has frustrated policymakers who see AI companies as inconsistent on regulation — opposing proposals at some points and supporting them at others, sources tell Axios.

  • OpenAI is "no longer seen as or acting as a leader in driving policy," one source close to the administration said, arguing researchers have "neutered" the company.
  • A White House official said OpenAI has been an incredible partner and pointed to the recent accord the company signed with the president.

Zoom out: It's not just OpenAI. Researchers also complicated Anthropic's efforts to strike a deal with the Pentagon after a clash between the company and senior administration officials earlier this year.

  • Employees at OpenAI, Anthropic and Google have signed high-profile letters at pivotal moments between companies and the government, including more than 1,000 who backed the viral "Pacing the Frontier" petition.
  • In a remarkable show of internal solidarity, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned and publicly blasted the company's safety practices — only to have several colleagues still inside Anthropic endorse his concerns.

Reality check: Executives have also adapted as political backlash to AI has grown and safety incidents have drawn more scrutiny, sources close to the companies say.

  • With some level of regulation seen as inevitable, companies have focused on molding the rules as favorably as possible rather than simply resisting them.

The bottom line: In the debate over AI safety and regulation, some researchers have become nearly as influential in setting the terms as OpenAI's Sam Altman or Anthropic's Dario Amodei.

item.title: "We're not asking for charity": Wikimedia CEO calls out AI for unpaid data use
item.description:
Wikipedia is starting to feel the effects of the AI-driven shift in how people find information, with page views falling 8% in the latest year, new Wikimedia Foundation CEO Bernadette Meehan told Axios.

Why it matters: Wikipedia is a crucial source of information for AI models, but those same models increasingly allow people to get Wikipedia-derived information without ever visiting the site — potentially threatening the ecosystem that keeps the online encyclopedia running.

Driving the news: Wikipedia page views declined 8% in 2025, and while the drop wasn't unexpected, "that doesn't mean that we're sort of starry-eyed about it and not concerned about it," Meehan said.

Follow the money: The problem is that even though generative AI systems rely heavily on Wikipedia's vast trove of human-created information, some companies won't pay for it, she said.

  • Wikimedia has a program that charges large-scale commercial users for reliable, high-volume access to its data. Publicly disclosed enterprise customers, whose payments make up 10% of the organization's operating expenses, include Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Perplexity and others.
  • OpenAI and Anthropic, two of the largest makers of generative AI models, aren't among Wikimedia's publicly disclosed enterprise customers. Meehan noted that Wikimedia has other agreements that aren't publicly disclosed and declined to identify those companies.
  • OpenAI and Anthropic both declined to comment.

What they're saying: Meehan, a former U.S. ambassador to Chile who took over Wikimedia's top job in January, said the reception from big technology companies has been mixed.

  • Some have embraced the idea that companies benefiting from Wikipedia should help sustain it. Others, she said, have acknowledged what Wikimedia considers excessive use of its data but declined to pay for enterprise access.
  • "We're not asking for charity," Meehan said.

Between the lines: There's an unusual economic tension here: Wikipedia makes its content freely available and has no intention of changing that, leaving it with limited leverage over AI companies that don't want to pay.

The big picture: Traffic matters to Wikimedia for reasons that go well beyond bragging rights for being one of the most popular destinations on the internet.

  • Roughly 80% of Wikimedia's operating budget comes from small donations, many prompted by banners shown to visitors to its site.
  • Readers also provide the pipeline for future Wikipedia editors. "If less readers are coming, that's less conversion to editors," Meehan said.

Ironically, Wikipedia has arguably never been more valuable to the broader information ecosystem.

  • "We're the backbone," Meehan said when asked about Wikipedia's importance to AI knowledge engines.

Meanwhile, Meehan is drawing a distinction between AI using Wikipedia and AI creating Wikipedia.

  • AI remains controversial among Wikipedia's volunteer communities, which set their own rules, but it is already being used for tasks such as translation, finding broken links and helping new editors spot problems with their contributions.

Meehan sees a clear boundary, though: AI should assist Wikipedia's human editors rather than replace them.

  • "I don't think you will ever see AI writing or generating Wikipedia articles," she said.
  • Asked whether she believes Wikipedia articles five years from now will still be written by humans for humans, Meehan replied: "I do."

Zoom out: Meehan also pointed out who and what gets left out if commercially developed AI becomes a principal gateway to knowledge.

  • Wikipedia exists in roughly 300 languages, including many that aren't likely to represent commercially attractive markets for AI companies.
  • She also raises the possibility of a knowledge divide in which the best access to information increasingly requires paying for an AI subscription.

The bottom line: Wikipedia spent the first phase of the generative AI boom becoming indispensable to AI. Its next challenge is ensuring that AI doesn't weaken the human and financial ecosystem that made Wikipedia indispensable in the first place.

Driving the news: Wikipedia page views declined 8% in 2025, and while the drop wasn't unexpected, "that doesn't mean that we're sort of starry-eyed about it and not concerned about it," Meehan said.

Follow the money: The problem is that even though generative AI systems rely heavily on Wikipedia's vast trove of human-created information, some companies won't pay for it, she said.

  • Wikimedia has a program that charges large-scale commercial users for reliable, high-volume access to its data. Publicly disclosed enterprise customers, whose payments make up 10% of the organization's operating expenses, include Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Perplexity and others.
  • OpenAI and Anthropic, two of the largest makers of generative AI models, aren't among Wikimedia's publicly disclosed enterprise customers. Meehan noted that Wikimedia has other agreements that aren't publicly disclosed and declined to identify those companies.
  • OpenAI and Anthropic both declined to comment.

What they're saying: Meehan, a former U.S. ambassador to Chile who took over Wikimedia's top job in January, said the reception from big technology companies has been mixed.

  • Some have embraced the idea that companies benefiting from Wikipedia should help sustain it. Others, she said, have acknowledged what Wikimedia considers excessive use of its data but declined to pay for enterprise access.
  • "We're not asking for charity," Meehan said.

Between the lines: There's an unusual economic tension here: Wikipedia makes its content freely available and has no intention of changing that, leaving it with limited leverage over AI companies that don't want to pay.

The big picture: Traffic matters to Wikimedia for reasons that go well beyond bragging rights for being one of the most popular destinations on the internet.

  • Roughly 80% of Wikimedia's operating budget comes from small donations, many prompted by banners shown to visitors to its site.
  • Readers also provide the pipeline for future Wikipedia editors. "If less readers are coming, that's less conversion to editors," Meehan said.

Ironically, Wikipedia has arguably never been more valuable to the broader information ecosystem.

  • "We're the backbone," Meehan said when asked about Wikipedia's importance to AI knowledge engines.

Meanwhile, Meehan is drawing a distinction between AI using Wikipedia and AI creating Wikipedia.

  • AI remains controversial among Wikipedia's volunteer communities, which set their own rules, but it is already being used for tasks such as translation, finding broken links and helping new editors spot problems with their contributions.

Meehan sees a clear boundary, though: AI should assist Wikipedia's human editors rather than replace them.

  • "I don't think you will ever see AI writing or generating Wikipedia articles," she said.
  • Asked whether she believes Wikipedia articles five years from now will still be written by humans for humans, Meehan replied: "I do."

Zoom out: Meehan also pointed out who and what gets left out if commercially developed AI becomes a principal gateway to knowledge.

  • Wikipedia exists in roughly 300 languages, including many that aren't likely to represent commercially attractive markets for AI companies.
  • She also raises the possibility of a knowledge divide in which the best access to information increasingly requires paying for an AI subscription.

The bottom line: Wikipedia spent the first phase of the generative AI boom becoming indispensable to AI. Its next challenge is ensuring that AI doesn't weaken the human and financial ecosystem that made Wikipedia indispensable in the first place.

item.title: Mortgage rates approach 3-year high as new applications plunge
item.description:
Mortgage rates spiked to their highest level in nearly three years, continuing their climb above the 7% threshold.

Why it matters: Housing sales were already slow due to a lack of inventory and elevated rates, creating a risk that the market could further its freeze.

Zoom in: The weekly average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 7.28% as of Thursday, Freddie Mac reported.

  • That's up 0.94 points from a year ago, and up 0.25 points from last week.
  • Mortgage rates closely track 10-year Treasury yields, which have risen by over 1.25 percentage points since the start of the Iran war in February.

The impact: Mortgage applications are plunging.

  • The Mortgage Bankers Association reported Wednesday that applications during the week ended Sept. 25 fell 6% from a week earlier.

With rates at their highest point since November 2023, home buyers are beginning to turn to adjustable-rate mortgages.

  • ARMs made up 10.3% of mortgage applications in the most recent period, marking the highest point since October 2025, according to MBA.
  • "Affordability and borrower demand have weakened in recent weeks as the higher-rate environment continues to put pressure on both prospective homebuyers and homeowners looking to refinance," MBA CEO Bob Broeksmit said in a statement.

What we're watching: There are early signs that rising rates could put downward pressure on prices as sellers look to attract buyers.

  • "Softer market conditions and greater affordability pressures have contributed to increased pricing pressures across many of our markets," KB Home senior VP William Hollinger said last week on an earnings call, noting the home builder had "made pricing adjustments."

Reality check: Rates may not remain elevated for long.

  • "We expect the situation to improve next year, as energy prices drop back and the aggressive Fed tightening cycle which has been priced into money markets does not fully materialise, causing mortgage rates to retrace most of their recent increases," Capital Economics senior North America economist Thomas Ryan wrote Tuesday.
  • Capital Economics projected that 30-year fixed mortgage rates would average 6.25% by the end of 2027.

item.title: Christa Pike's execution failed. Here's how lethal injection works
item.description:
Lethal injections are under scrutiny after Christa Pike survived two rounds of drugs during Tennessee's failed attempt to execute her.

Why it matters: Lethal injection has been the dominant U.S. execution method for decades, accounting for roughly 89% of the 1,683 executions carried out since 1976, per the Death Penalty Information Center.

Driving the news: Pike, convicted of killing a classmate three decades ago, survived two rounds of lethal injection drugs Wednesday in what would have been the state's first execution of a woman in 200 years.

  • In response, Gov. Bill Lee halted executions and ordered a "comprehensive, third-party review" of the failed attempt.
  • Pike's execution attempt followed hours of legal whiplash in which courts first stayed the execution before reversing course.
  • Pike is still alive as of Thursday afternoon, her attorney said at a news conference, according to the AP. She is receiving "lifesaving care" after a failed attempt Wednesday night that her attorney said amounted to "torture."

The big picture: Execution protocols vary by state, but lethal injections generally follow the same basic process.

Here's what to know.

Update: The map labels were changed to consolidate primary and secondary execution methods. Data: Death Penalty Information Center; Note: New Hampshire abolished the death penalty but retains one prisoner on death row; Map: Erin Davis/Axios

Why states adopted lethal injection

Flashback: Lethal injections emerged after the Supreme Court allowed capital punishment to return in the 1970s.

  • Oklahoma became the first state to authorize the practice in 1977. Texas carried out its first five years later.
  • Before lethal injections, states commonly used methods like electrocution, gas, hanging and firing squads. Lawmakers considered injections to be less violent and cheaper.

Lethal injections are now used in all death penalty states.

  • The Supreme Court requires states to reserve the death penalty only for the most heinous murders.

Several states — Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah — allow firing squads.

  • Idaho made firing squad its primary execution method in July.

How lethal injections are administered

There isn't one standard procedure. States use different protocols, but the basic process is similar.

  • A fatal dose of drugs is delivered through an IV while the prisoner is restrained, often to a gurney.
  • Arizona, for example, requires two IV catheters, one as a backup in case the first line fails.

Physicians often don't administer lethal injections because the American Medical Association's Code of Medical Ethics says doctors should not participate in executions.

  • States instead sometimes rely on execution teams that can include prison guards, corrections employees and other personnel trained to administer the drugs.

What drugs are used in lethal injections

How it works: There are two main ways these drugs are administered.

  • One drug path — The state administers a sedative or barbiturate, commonly pentobarbital, to cause death.
  • Three drug path — Another method includes giving a sedative or anesthetic, then a paralytic before a final drug stops the heart.

Yes, but: Pentobarbital itself is controversial, with critics questioning whether it really causes a painless death.

  • A Justice Department review under the Biden administration cited concerns that the drug possibly caused pain and suffering.
  • President Trump's DOJ reauthorized the federal use of pentobarbital.

Lethal injections don't always work as planned

Pike's case is not the first lethal injection gone wrong. The DPIC says 75 of 1,054 lethal injections (about 7%) were botched from 1890 to 2010 — the most of any method.

What they're saying: Witnesses to some executions have described prisoners gasping for air and struggling to breathe.

  • Some prisoners survive the initial attempt but later die from complications or other medical causes, sometimes linked to the execution attempt. Others are executed at a later date.
  • Autopsies have found evidence of prisoner suffering from pulmonary edema, which is a buildup of fluid in the lungs that can create the same sensation as drowning, per NPR.

Case in point: In 2022, Alabama called off Kenneth Smith's execution after officials couldn't insert an IV before his death warrant expired.

  • Smith survived but was later executed in 2024 through nitrogen hypoxia, a first in American history.
  • In 2014, the execution of Clayton Lockett in Oklahoma went badly after officials failed to properly establish an IV. He died nearly an hour later.

Go deeper: America is seeing an uptick in executions

item.title: The Fed's long-term interest rate problem
item.description:
The relentless rise in long-term interest rates is starting to have effects on more parts of the economy, Kansas City Fed president Jeff Schmid told Axios Thursday.

  • "You're starting to see some friction in some of the long-market users of credit," he said, pointing to multifamily housing and commercial lending.
  • "Even on the mortgage rate side, it's starting to affect home prices, which is how the price of credit works relative to valuation," Schmid said at a conference on investing in rural America hosted by the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond in Asheville, N.C.

The big picture: Schmid spoke alongside Richmond Fed president Tom Barkin and Boston Fed president Susan Collins, who weighed in on the forces driving the rise in borrowing costs.

  • "I think you're seeing this trillion-dollar AI buildout, and I think it's not surprising that rates go up if you've got a lot more demand out there," Barkin added.

Collins said AI investment is also helping drive the solid economic growth that has persisted despite higher borrowing costs.

  • "I think it does have broader effects, not just in particular sectors," Collins said. But it "remains to be seen" whether investment will continue at its current pace, she added.

The intrigue: Schmid likened the Fed's challenge of separating strong demand from supply-driven inflation to a seven-layer dip — one of his favorite foods.

  • "The beauty of a seven-layer dip is you have equal amounts of beans and sour cream," Schmid said. Right now, with AI and data centers, "there's too much beans in that dip," he added.
  • "And not enough chips!" quipped Barkin.

item.title: Trump, Big AI go all-in together
item.description:
President Trump and the AI industry have co-signed one of the biggest economic and technological wagers of all time.

  • If it goes right: A new age of abundance — explosive productivity, staggering wealth and a generational leap in American power.
  • If it goes wrong: A catastrophic bust that destroys capital and jobs and, in the words of several involved, threatens widespread human harm.

Why it matters: Neither Trump nor the AI titans have plausible deniability. Their fortunes have become so tightly bound that success will be shared — and failure impossible to disown.

The big picture: Trump and Big AI have fused their futures around four enormous bets.

1. The economic bet: That trillions poured into chips, data centers and power will create a productivity engine powerful enough to fuel a new Industrial Revolution.

  • AI infrastructure spending is projected to reach $10.3 trillion by 2032, but the payoff remains unproven: One analysis found hyperscalers have spent nearly $1 trillion more on AI since 2024 than AI has generated in revenue.
  • The promise sold by Trump and his tech allies is a new era of growth and abundance. The peril is a historic misallocation of capital on a scale few industries have ever seen.

2. The regulation bet: That Washington can clear the runway for an AI takeoff while leaving the companies largely responsible for policing themselves.

  • The new White House accord signed by Trump and the AI giants enshrines voluntary safeguards, company-led testing and third-party reviews instead of new federal mandates.
  • The promise is American dominance over China. The peril is that self-regulation fails, forcing Washington to intervene only after damage has already been inflicted.

3. The safety bet: That AI can grow vastly more powerful without becoming vastly harder to control.

  • Many of the most dire safety warnings come from AI researchers themselves. Anthropic's own IPO prospectus contemplates scenarios in which advanced AI kills humanity.
  • The promise is almost limitless: superintelligent systems that help cure diseases and accelerate scientific discovery. The peril is self-improving AI that evolves faster than its creators can comprehend or contain.

4. The political bet: That Trump and Big AI can become inseparable without making each other even more toxic.

  • Trump has staked his legacy on winning the AI race — dismissing fears about data centers costing Republicans in the midterms — while the industry has staked billions on the policy environment he's creating.
  • The promise is that Trump and Big AI become partners in the defining technological transformation of the century. The peril is that every AI failure, disruption or backlash becomes a liability they share.

The bottom line: Trump and the AI industry are asking the country for a leap of faith at a uniquely fragile moment for both.

  • Americans are deeply dissatisfied with both the economy and Trump's presidency, with his approval rating plunging to record lows ahead of a potentially disastrous midterm season.
  • The AI industry faces an even more basic credibility problem: A new Quinnipiac poll found 74% of Americans lack trust in AI executives, while only 34% believe AI will do more good than harm in their daily lives.

item.title: Trump and CEOs try to shed AI's toxic branding
item.description:
The great AI rebranding is on, led by President Trump and tech titans like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who are embracing an alternative term: "super intelligence," or SI.

Why it matters: Leaders in D.C. and Silicon Valley are worried the public backlash against AI and data centers will hamper the development of this staggeringly powerful and existentially dangerous technology. The new label is part of a broader effort to shift the narrative.

Driving the news: Flanked by the most powerful figures in tech on Tuesday, Trump officially declared "super intelligence" the preferred terminology of the executive branch. He'd previously solicited alternative terms for AI on Truth Social.

  • "Now we're calling it, again, super. We can say the word super, because the other word is a fake word," Trump said after Tuesday's White House summit. Leaders from Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, xAI and Nvidia all signed the "White House Accord on Super Intelligence."
  • Huang has recently extended the label to physical infrastructure, referring to data centers as "super intelligence factories." Opposition to the huge, energy-guzzling facilities is dimming the prospects for fast-growing AI firms and some congressional candidates.

Between the lines: A rose by any other name would smell as sweet, and AI by any other name will likely seem as scary.

  • Communities are building bipartisan coalitions against data centers, younger workers are anxious about their career prospects, and AI insiders continue to warn about catastrophic risks, notes Axios Communicators author Simon Hernandez-Arthur.
  • Calling it "super intelligence" attempts to evoke the technology's promise without immediately bringing to mind all that negative baggage.

What they're saying: Some of the tech executives who appeared with Trump continued to use "AI" in their remarks, but xAI CEO Elon Musk caught himself and pivoted to "SI." Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has long used "superintelligence" branding.

  • Huang, CEO of the world's most valuable company, appears to be leading the charge. He used the term twice in a post and repeatedly invoked it in a panel discussion at the White House. When he slipped once and said "AI," Huang corrected himself: "I am going to get good at this."
  • AI company representatives declined to comment about the name change on the record. Some said their companies were generally supportive of the rebrand and plan to use "SI" when meeting with the president and working with the federal government. Others said they didn't expect it to catch fire outside of those contexts.
  • One source compared it to Trump's renaming of the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America, which many (though not all) oil executives adopted in their external and internal communications.

By the numbers: "SI" has yet to catch on with the public. A YouGov poll conducted this week found that 53% of respondents considered "artificial intelligence" the better term for the tech, vs. 9% who preferred "super intelligence."

The bottom line: Trump said on Tuesday that "artificial" intelligence made the technology sound like a hoax: "The name is now super intelligence. That's not a hoax, in fact it's the exact opposite."

  • Polls suggest most Americans agree with him that AI is anything but a hoax. That's why they're so worried.

item.title: Netanyahu says FlyDubai pilots prevented a "9/11 disaster"
item.description:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu revealed new details about a FlyDubai flight bound for Israel during which a pilot stabbed a colleague, sending the plane spiraling thousands of feet.

The big picture: Netanyahu told CNN Wednesday evening that the Indian pilot who was stabbed, Capt. Smit Machchhar, unlocked the cockpit after being attacked and an Israeli passenger who works as a plumber, Yaniv Hayun, entered and found the Omani pilot apparently trying to interfere with the aircraft's controls.

  • Netanyahu said the suspect was being interrogated in Saudi Arabia and that the UAE agreed Israel could participate in the interrogation.

What they're saying: The Israeli prime minister told CNN's Jim Sciutto that passengers heard shouts and screams coming from the cockpit and that the plumber saw the attacking pilot hovering over the instruments, noting "he was trying to jam the instruments."

item.title: Fed watchdog clears former chair Powell in renovation probe
item.description:
A Federal Reserve watchdog found no criminal wrongdoing by former chair Jerome Powell in its investigation of the central bank's expensive headquarters renovation, according to a report released on Wednesday.

Why it matters: The findings effectively clear Powell after the Justice Department opened an unprecedented criminal investigation into then-Fed chair, which became public in January.

What they're saying: "At no point during our evaluation did we find reasonable grounds to believe that a violation of federal criminal law had occurred requiring a referral to the U.S. Attorney General," the Office of Inspector General wrote in the report.

  • The watchdog added that it "did not identify administrative misconduct during our evaluation."

Yes, but: While the report clears Powell, it faults Fed management and oversight of the project as construction costs more than doubled to $2.5 billion.

  • The Fed "did not take numerous actions available to it that could have better controlled costs and mitigated some of the significant construction cost increases," the report says.

Flashback: The renovation became a flashpoint in President Trump's broader campaign against Powell and the Fed.

  • Trump toured the construction site with Powell in July 2025 and publicly challenged him over the project's soaring costs.

Zoom out: The Justice Department's investigation centered on Powell's June 2025 testimony to Congress about the renovation and its rising costs.

  • Powell denied wrongdoing and argued at the time that the investigation was part of a broader effort to pressure the Fed over interest rates.
  • DOJ closed the investigation in April as the Fed's inspector general continued its review.

Zoom in: The watchdog said that inflation alone could not explain the project's higher costs.

  • For instance, the report shows that two major mechanical, electrical and plumbing contracts more than tripled to $539 million from an earlier $178 million estimate, far outpacing the broader rise in construction costs.

Of note: The report says that the key design features that drew scrutiny from Congress and other critics — including marble, water features and a garden terrace — did not materially contribute to the project's cost increases.

  • The Fed removed four planned new fountains in June 2025 because officials worried about "external stakeholders, such as Congress and the media, raising concerns about the design," according to the report.

Friction point: The president, in a Truth Social post in response to the report, said that Powell "should be forced to resign, IMMEDIATELY! If he doesn't resign, he should be sued, at the highest level, by the United States Government."

What to watch: Powell has remained on the Fed's board after his term as chair ended in May — an unusual move that he said was tied to seeing the investigation through to its conclusion.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with President Trump's comments.

item.title: Google unveils long-awaited Gemini 4
item.description:
Google is unveiling its long-awaited next-generation AI model, Gemini 4 Argon, to a small group of cybersecurity partners, the company said Wednesday.

Why it matters: Gemini 4 arrives after a long gap at the top of Google's model lineup, in which the company kept rolling out smaller, cheaper Flash models while rivals OpenAI and Anthropic sprinted forward.

State of play: Google says Gemini 4 Argon is built to handle complex, long-running tasks in software engineering, finance, legal work and cybersecurity.

  • Google said the new model is state of the art on certain coding and knowledge work benchmarks, outperforming competing OpenAI frontier model GPT-6 Astra on several.
  • The company is rolling the model out only to a group of trusted cybersecurity defenders and is participating in the U.S. government's voluntary prerelease process.
  • Google says it will expand access after additional testing, with paying subscribers first in line.

What they're saying: "Argon is a well-rounded model that has frontier capabilities across several domains," Tulsee Doshi, head of Gemini products at Google DeepMind, told Axios.

  • "We've seen strong performance up close as Googlers have put the model through its paces in recent weeks, with many relying on it for their hardest coding and research problems."

Yes, but: Bloomberg reported Wednesday, citing anonymous sources, that some of those employees found the model's performance lacking in internal testing. (The company told Bloomberg that was inaccurate.)

  • This is the challenge with benchmarks: Models can be trained to perform well on them, but the real testing and results come in the real word.

Flashback: Gemini 4 comes out nearly a year after the previous flagship model generation, Gemini 3.

  • In May, Google CEO Sundar Pichai said the company's next major model release would come in June.
  • That model, widely expected to be Gemini 3.5 Pro, never came out.
  • In July, Axios reported that poor morale among Google DeepMind employees was part of the reason for the delay.

Zoom in: Google's additional time investment may not be viewed as negatively in the context of the AI safety debate that has embroiled companies and users.

  • OpenAI has had issues with agents going rogue, and recently said it is scrapping GPT-6.1 Astra due to security issues.
  • Top AI developers OpenAI and Anthropic are investigating tens of thousands of incidents involving their agents misbehaving, Axios previously reported.

The bottom line: If the developer community finds Gemini 4 to be as competitive with OpenAI's and Anthropic's frontier systems as the benchmarks indicate, it would result in a massive catch-up for an AI company some had started to doubt.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional reports on the model's performance.
